messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 80
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Social Worker
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 66

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Male Presence: Being alone with men, Known People: Related people, Auditory (Door): Doors opening or slamming
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Dreams: Situations or times of day that tend to bring on nightmares, Memory Erasure: I try to erase the memory of the event, Meaning Seeking: I think about why the event has happened to me
  Threat: Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order, Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind., Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
  Negative Appraisals: Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened, Mistrust: People can't be trusted

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Clinical Vignette: Margaret

Margaret Kowalski is an eighty-year-old Polish-American woman who has spent the last fifty-three years as a clinical social worker, first in hospital settings and latterly in community mental health. She came to her first appointment in early November, referred by her primary care physician after Margaret disclosed to him that she had not slept properly in six weeks. Her PCL-5 score of 66 placed her firmly in the severe range for PTSD, though she had never named it as such until now.

The trauma itself occurred when Margaret was twenty-seven years old. She had been engaged to Thomas, a man she had known since childhood through Polish community circles in Pittsburgh. They had been together for four years when, in the spring of 1971, an argument about wedding plans escalated in his apartment. Thomas had been drinking. When Margaret said she wanted to postpone the wedding, he struck her across the face, then again, then threw her against the kitchen counter. The sequence of it remained fractured in her mind—not a coherent narrative but a series of isolated, vivid snapshots: his hand raised, the sound of her own cry, the cold edge of the countertop against her ribs, his voice saying things she could no longer recall in order. What stayed with her most vividly was the moment the door to his apartment swung open behind him as neighbors came to help her; the sudden intrusion of light and voices, and Thomas's silhouette in the doorway. She had left him that day and never returned.

For decades, Margaret had managed. She had built a career helping others, married briefly to a gentle man who died in 1989, and created a life of deliberate structure. But in recent months, something had shifted. She had begun to notice that she could not enter a room without immediately identifying the exits—a habit so ingrained she had stopped thinking of it as unusual until her colleague at the community center mentioned it. She found herself avoiding situations where she might be alone with male clients, redirecting appointments to younger female social workers with explanations that felt increasingly thin. She had taken to sleeping in her living room because the bedroom felt too enclosed, too far from the front door. When she did sleep, nightmares came—not full dreams but flashes, the same snapshots repeating. She had begun avoiding the hours just before dusk, when she knew sleep might come, staying up instead watching television until exhaustion forced her under.

What had finally compelled her to seek help was an incident at the senior center where she volunteers. A male volunteer, a kind man named Robert whom she had known for two years, had come up behind her to ask about a filing system. When he placed his hand on her shoulder, Margaret had flinched so violently that she knocked over a stack of folders. Robert had apologized profusely, confused by her reaction. In that moment, standing among scattered papers, Margaret had felt the full weight of what had happened to her—not as history, but as a present, inescapable fact.

She had come to believe, over the decades, that the world was fundamentally unsafe, that people could not be trusted no matter how long you knew them or how gentle they appeared. The attack had shattered her sense of how the world worked. She felt contaminated by what Thomas had done to her, as though the violence had left something permanent and dirty on her skin that no amount of time could wash away. She found herself thinking obsessively about why it had happened—what she had said or done that had provoked him, what she might have done differently. These thoughts offered no answers, only a cycling sense of culpability that she knew, intellectually, was irrational, but which felt absolutely true.

Margaret sits in the consulting room with her hands folded in her lap, her silver hair neatly pinned, her posture impeccable. She is articulate and reflective, a woman accustomed to observing human suffering in others. But her eyes are exhausted, and there is a tremor in her voice when she speaks about the sleeplessness, about the way her body now betrays her by reacting to men she consciously knows mean no harm. She is afraid that at eighty, she has run out of time to heal from this, that the trauma has simply waited all these years for her defenses to weaken. What she hopes for, though she barely dares to say it, is that she might be able to be alone in a room again without her body flooding with alarm.
